title: Ranking, Ordering & Data Sufficiency
relevance: Ranking, ordering, and data-sufficiency items are staples of campus aptitude OAs and early SDE screens because they test careful end-to-end reasoning under incomplete information.

phases.goal: Establish the core rank↔total conversion formulas and the five standard Data Sufficiency answer choices.

must_hit.point: In a linear sequence, Total equals (rank from top) + (rank from bottom) − 1 (equivalently Left + Right − 1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States Total = Left + Right − 1 or Top + Bottom − 1 and can apply it to get 14 + 23 − 1 = 36.

must_hit.point: For two sorted indices A < B, the number of people strictly between them is B − A − 1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Quotes Between = B − A − 1 for non-overlapping positions.

must_hit.point: Data Sufficiency questions use five fixed options: (a) I alone, (b) II alone, (c) both together necessary, (d) each alone sufficient, (e) both together still insufficient.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Correctly restates what (a)–(e) mean without inventing extra choices.

probes: How do you convert a person’s ranks from both ends of a row into the total length of the row?
What are the five standard Data Sufficiency answer choices, and what does each one claim?

hints.1: Think about how one person is counted once from each end.
hints.2: Write Total in terms of the two end-ranks, then list what (a) through (e) each assert about statements I and II.
hints.3: Total = Left + Right − 1; Between = B − A − 1; and (a)–(e) are I alone / II alone / both needed / each alone / still insufficient.

phases.goal: Show how to apply rank formulas under swaps and overlaps, build comparison chains, and evaluate DS statements for uniqueness.

must_hit.point: After two people interchange, the swapped position can be known from both ends at once, so Total = that Left rank + that Right rank − 1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains that after the swap, Q’s original spot is 25th from left and 21st from right, so Total = 25 + 21 − 1 = 45.

must_hit.point: When Left + Right > Total, the two people cross; people strictly between them equal (Left + Right) − Total − 2.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Flags the overlap case (e.g. 22 + 26 = 48 > 40) and applies 48 − 40 − 2 = 6.

must_hit.point: Comparison and finish-order puzzles are solved by inserting each clue into one strict chain before naming tallest, median, heaviest, or last.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Builds a single order such as C > D > A > E > B, X > V > W > Y > Z, Q > S > T > R > P, or R > P > Q > S > T.

must_hit.point: For Data Sufficiency, test I alone, then II alone, then both; data is sufficient only if exactly one unique answer remains.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows cases like digits 7 and 2 leaving both 72 and 27, so I+II are still insufficient, versus mother–son ages where together k = 10 and M = 50.

probes: If Left + Right exceeds Total, how do you count people sitting between the two persons?
Walk me through how you decide among (a)–(e) when each statement may or may not pin down a unique value.

hints.1: Check whether the two end-ranks can describe the same person after a swap, and whether the positions overlap.
hints.2: For DS, never combine early: finish I alone, finish II alone, then intersect; reject any case that still has multiple values.
hints.3: Overlap between-count is (Left + Right) − Total − 2; sufficiency requires a single answer (multiple survivors ⇒ insufficient).

phases.goal: Contrast which formula or DS verdict applies under overlapping ranks, independent statements, and yes/no questions.

must_hit.point: Non-overlap uses B − A − 1 style between-counts; overlap (Left + Right > Total) switches to (Left + Right) − Total − 2.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly compares the two regimes and when Left + Right exceeding Total forces the overlap formula.

must_hit.point: (c) both-together necessary is not the same as (d) each alone sufficient: if I and II each independently yield a unique answer, the choice is (d).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites the pattern where Rahul’s rank is 30th from I alone and 15th from II alone, so the answer is each alone, not both-together.

must_hit.point: For yes/no Data Sufficiency, a definitive NO is as sufficient as a definitive YES; only ambiguity fails.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that settling “Is C High Value?” with NO (lifetime spending 4750 does not exceed 5000) still makes the combined data sufficient.

probes: How do you choose between the ordinary between-formula and the overlap formula?
If statement I alone works, why must you still test statement II before picking (c) versus (d)?

hints.1: Compare Left + Right to Total, and remember to finish both statement tests.
hints.2: Overlap flips the between formula; independent unique answers from I and from II mean (d), not (c).
hints.3: Left + Right > Total ⇒ (Left + Right) − Total − 2; each-alone ⇒ (d); a clear NO still counts as answering a yes/no DS item.

phases.goal: Apply ranking and DS reasoning to OA-style product-ranking and High-Value classification prompts.

must_hit.point: Inserting new products ranked above X worsens X’s top rank but leaves X’s bottom rank unchanged, because the set of worse performers is unchanged.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that after 35 products are added above X, bottom rank stays 428th even though top rank becomes 112 + 35 = 147th.

must_hit.point: Partial purchase averages can be combined to answer a High-Value yes/no even when the answer is NO, as long as the truth value is unique.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Combines 10 × 350 = 3500 and 5 × 250 = 1250 into 4750, notes 4750 does not exceed 5000, and concludes both together suffice with a definitive NO.

probes: New higher-ranked products are added above X—what happens to X’s rank from the bottom, and why?
In a yes/no High-Value DS question, is a definitive NO enough to call the data sufficient?

hints.1: Ask which side of X the new items land on, and what “sufficient” means for a yes/no.
hints.2: Items above X only change the count of better performers; for High Value, sum known purchase blocks and compare to the threshold.
hints.3: Bottom rank stays 428th; 3500 + 1250 = 4750 < 5000 ⇒ definitive NO ⇒ combined statements are sufficient.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: If the positions do not cross, people between follow B − A − 1; if Left + Right > Total, they overlap and the count is (Left + Right) − Total − 2 (the −2 excludes the two people themselves).

tradeoffs.topic: Both statements together (c) vs each statement alone (d)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Always finish testing I alone and II alone; if each independently produces a unique answer, choose (d). Choose (c) only when neither alone works but the pair together does.

tradeoffs.topic: Top-rank change vs bottom-rank stability when better items are inserted
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Adding items ranked above X increases X’s rank-from-top, but the number of worse performers is unchanged, so rank-from-bottom stays the same.

gotchas.trap: When Left + Right > Total, forgetting the −2 while counting people between the two positions.
gotchas.correction: People strictly between equal (Left + Right) − Total − 2; the −2 removes the two people themselves.

gotchas.trap: Calling Data Sufficiency “sufficient” when more than one value still fits (e.g. 72 and 27).
gotchas.correction: Sufficient means exactly one unique answer; multiple surviving values mean the data is insufficient.

gotchas.trap: Stopping after statement I works and selecting (c) without testing statement II alone.
gotchas.correction: Test II separately; if II also answers alone, the correct choice is (d) each alone is sufficient.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a yes/no Data Sufficiency item is sufficient only if the answer is YES.
gotchas.correction: A definitive NO is also sufficient; you need one unambiguous truth value, not specifically YES.
